title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
This is the end of §96 and Scholion 2 (§97), the last page of E449. The paper's frame is power residues: for a prime P = λn+1, the λ-th powers give only n distinct residues mod P. So there are p, q with P | p^λ − q^λ but P ∤ p − q. Then P divides the cyclotomic quotient Φ_λ(p,q) = (p^λ − q^λ)/(p − q).

The end of §96 (λ=5) uses the identity Φ_5(p,−q) = p^4 − p^3q + p^2q^2 − pq^3 + q^4 = (p^2 − ½pq + q^2)^2 − 5(½pq)^2, written by Euler with ∓ for both signs. So f^2 − 5g^2 ≡ 0 (mod P) with g ≢ 0, hence 5 is a quadratic residue mod every prime 5n+1.

§97 does the same for λ=7. Φ_7(p,q) = p^6 + p^5q + … + q^6 = (p^3 + ½p^2q − ½pq^2 − q^3)^2 + 7(½p^2q + ½pq^2)^2. Equivalently, 4Φ_7 = (2p^3 + p^2q − pq^2 − 2q^3)^2 + 7(pq(p+q))^2. Hence some f^2 + 7g^2 is divisible by P = 7n+1, so −7 is a quadratic residue mod P.

Euler notes that this agrees with his earlier empirical conjecture (essentially quadratic reciprocity) stated before in the paper. In modern terms: if P ≡ 1 (mod 7) then (−7/P) = 1, consistent with (−7/P) = (P/7). These are the λ=5 and λ=7 instances of Gauss's identity 4Φ_ℓ(x,y) = Y^2 − (−1)^{(ℓ−1)/2} ℓ Z^2, i.e. of the quadratic subfield Q(√ℓ*) of the ℓ-th cyclotomic field.
errors: No algebraic error. I expanded the identity: the squared term contributes coefficients 1, 1, −3/4, −5/2, −3/4, 1, 1; adding 7B^2 = (7/4)p^4q^2 + (7/2)p^3q^3 + (7/4)p^2q^4 gives all coefficients equal to 1. The λ=5 identity also checks.

Minor gap left implicit: one must also know P ∤ g, so that f^2 ≡ −7g^2 really makes −7 a residue. If P | pq(p+q), then either P | p or q (excluded, since the residues come from powers of units), or p ≡ −q, in which case Φ_7 ≡ q^6 ≢ 0. So the gap is easily closed, but Euler does not say this.

Euler's argument gives only one direction (P ≡ 1 mod 7 ⇒ −7 is a residue). Other primes in the residue classes the conjecture predicts are not covered, so it only 'confirms' a special case of the conjecture.

ideas.what: Decomposition of the 7th cyclotomic form: 4Φ_7(p,q) = (2p^3 + p^2q − pq^2 − 2q^3)^2 + 7(p^2q + pq^2)^2
ideas.modern_name: Gauss's identity 4Φ_ℓ = Y^2 − (−1)^{(ℓ−1)/2} ℓ Z^2 (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae art. 357); quadratic subfield Q(√−7) of Q(ζ_7)

ideas.what: Use of λ-th power residues (n distinct residues mod λn+1) to produce a prime divisor of Φ_λ(p,q), then reading off a quadratic residue
ideas.modern_name: Splitting of primes ≡1 mod ℓ in Q(ζ_ℓ), hence in its quadratic subfield; special cases of quadratic reciprocity
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (power-residue counting); Gauss/Lagrange for reciprocity proofs
ideas.where_published: E449; the reciprocity conjecture appears in E164 and in E552

ideas.what: Proof that 5 is a QR mod primes 5n+1 and −7 is a QR mod primes 7n+1
ideas.modern_name: Partial cases of quadratic reciprocity for 5 and −7
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler/Lagrange (1775, Recherches d'arithmétique, for small cases); Gauss in general

missed.claim: Euler explicitly writes down the ℓ=5 and ℓ=7 cases of the identity usually called Gauss's identity 4Φ_ℓ = Y^2 ∓ ℓZ^2, 27 years before the Disquisitiones. He uses them for exactly Gauss's purpose: proving (±ℓ/P) = 1 for P ≡ 1 mod ℓ. Some reciprocity histories (e.g. Lemmermeyer) may note this, but general references attribute the identity to Gauss alone.
missed.quote: haec vero expreſſio reducitur ad hanc formam: (p^3+½ppq−½pqq−q^3)^2+7(½ppq+½pqq)^2
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a priority/attribution detail for the cyclotomic quadratic-subfield identity. It is likely known to specialist historians of reciprocity, so it is only modestly new.

missed.claim: Euler does the cases ℓ=5 and ℓ=7 by ad hoc completion of squares and stops ('Simili modo'). He does not state the general pattern for ℓ=11, 13, …, which Gauss later obtained via Gauss sums and periods.
missed.quote: Simili modo si poteſtates ſeptimae per numerum primum 7n+1 diuidantur
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is historically interesting as a near-miss of the general theorem; mathematically it has been superseded.

deep.surprise_reason: The explicit ℓ=7 instance of Gauss's identity in 1774, used for a reciprocity case, is a genuine precursor. It is in a published paper and probably known to reciprocity historians, so it is only mildly surprising.
transcription_corrections: The 'p^5q' term is partly obscured by an ink mark in the scan; the reading p^6+p^5q+... is correct.
